paragraphs: Distributed learning must combine work from machines that can differ in computing power, communication reliability, and the amount of data they hold. These differences make coordination part of the optimization problem. This paper develops an asynchronous algorithm for nonsmooth learning problems, allowing distributed computation to proceed despite uneven communication and computation.

The method is designed to be adjustable across several practical conditions: expensive communication, unequal machine speeds, and uneven data distribution. That flexibility matters because a single coordination pattern may suit one distributed setting poorly even if it works well in another. The paper both proposes the algorithm and analyzes its convergence behavior.

The central guarantee is linear convergence with a fixed learning rate that does not depend on communication delays or the number of machines. Within the analyzed setting, delays can slow progress but cannot destroy convergence. This separates speed from eventual reliability: delayed information may make learning take longer, while the algorithm still retains its convergence guarantee without choosing a delay-dependent learning rate.
icml-2018-a-delay-tolerant-proximal-grad.tldr: An asynchronous optimization algorithm tolerates communication delays while retaining linear convergence with a fixed, delay-independent learning rate.

paragraphs: The paper studies a signal whose value stays constant over stretches and changes at particular locations. Its goal goes beyond finding those change points: it also identifies the levels associated with clusters. This connects locating boundaries with deciding which observations belong together in a model of the signal.

The authors formulate the task as penalized least-squares selection among models indexed by partitions of the observation locations. The fit term rewards agreement with the data, while the penalty influences which partition is selected. Minimizing this criterion approximates a maximum a-posteriori estimator, connecting the optimization problem to Bayesian model selection. A computationally efficient algorithm approximately solves the problem.

The statistical analysis establishes an oracle inequality, which compares the estimator’s performance with a suitable benchmark among the candidate models. From it, the authors derive conditions for consistency and an adaptive upper bound on expected squared error. These results motivate the approximation statistically. Simulated-data experiments then examine the guarantees and illustrate how the algorithm behaves.
icml-2018-bayesian-model-selection-for-c.tldr: The paper combines change-point detection and clustering through approximate Bayesian model selection, supported by statistical error guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper asks how network architecture limits the accuracy with which a feedforward neural network can approximate a function. It studies networks with piecewise linear activation functions. The focus is on mathematical constraints on representation: how much network capacity is required to reach a particular approximation error.

The first contribution establishes lower bounds on network size that account for approximation error, depth, and width. A lower bound identifies a minimum requirement, so it helps distinguish what an architecture could plausibly represent from what is too demanding for its size. For certain function classes, including strongly convex functions, these bounds improve on earlier results.

The second contribution considers two networks with identical weights but different activation functions and bounds the difference between them. This addresses the effect of changing the activation while holding the learned parameters fixed. Together, the results examine two sources of representational behavior: the amount and arrangement of network capacity, and the activation functions used to transform information.
icml-2018-bounds-on-the-approximation-po.tldr: The paper bounds the network size needed for function approximation and the effect of changing activations while keeping weights fixed.

paragraphs: A learning agent’s performance depends both on its behavior and on the environment in which it acts. In some problems, a limited set of environmental parameters can also be adjusted. This paper introduces Configurable Markov Decision Processes to represent that additional opportunity within the learning problem.

The accompanying algorithm, Safe Policy-Model Iteration, jointly and adaptively optimizes the agent’s policy and the environment configuration. A policy determines how the agent acts; the configuration determines the adjustable aspects of its surroundings. Treating them together makes their interaction part of the optimization, allowing the learning process to consider improvements through either kind of choice.

The authors derive theoretical results for the approach and evaluate it on two illustrative problems. Those experiments show benefits from environmental configurability for the learned policy’s performance. The contribution therefore concerns settings where some environmental control is actually available: it provides a framework and algorithm for using that control alongside policy learning, with experimental evidence that the combination can be useful.
icml-2018-configurable-markov-decision-p.tldr: Configurable Markov Decision Processes let an agent jointly improve its policy and the adjustable parts of its environment.

paragraphs: Large datasets create a need to select representative elements without repeatedly working over every available item. This paper studies summarization through submodularity, a diminishing-returns property: an additional item contributes less when much of its value is already covered. That structure makes it possible to seek strong approximate solutions efficiently.

The framework has two stages. First, training functions guide the reduction of the original set of candidate items. Later, new functions are optimized over that smaller set. The objective is to retain nearly the value available from the complete set. A key condition is that the new functions come from the same distribution as the training functions.

The authors develop streaming and distributed algorithms for this problem and provide theoretical guarantees. These approaches address how the first-stage reduction can be performed at scale, while preserving usefulness for later optimization. Experiments on image summarization and ride-share optimization demonstrate utility and efficiency in those applications, supporting the practical value of preparing a smaller candidate set for subsequent tasks.
icml-2018-data-summarization-at-scale-a-.tldr: Streaming and distributed algorithms learn smaller candidate sets that preserve value for later submodular optimization tasks drawn from the same distribution.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization across a connected network where a global objective is the sum of local functions. The relevant objectives have diminishing returns, giving structure to an otherwise nonconvex problem. The aim is to obtain a strong global solution using computation and communication available locally at the network’s nodes.

The proposed Decentralized Continuous Greedy algorithm uses message passing to achieve the tight approximation factor 1−1/e for the studied continuous submodular setting. This is an approximation guarantee relative to the global optimum. The analysis also bounds convergence in terms of network size and spectral properties of the topology, connecting optimization progress to the structure of communication.

The authors then use continuous optimization to handle discrete submodular problems. Local discrete functions are extended to continuous domains, the decentralized method coordinates optimization, and a suitable rounding procedure returns a discrete solution. With proper rounding, the resulting consensus algorithm retains the same tight approximation factor. This provides a shared route to decentralized solutions in both settings.
icml-2018-decentralized-submodular-maxim.tldr: A decentralized message-passing algorithm achieves a tight submodular approximation guarantee and extends from continuous to discrete optimization through relaxation and rounding.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for training neural networks with certifiable robustness to adversarial perturbations. The central aim is to make robustness something supported by a guarantee within the method’s scope. Training is based on abstract interpretation, which supplies the framework for reasoning about the network’s behavior under perturbation.

The authors present several abstract transformers that trade off computational efficiency and precision. These alternatives matter because a robustness analysis must be informative enough to support certification while remaining practical to use during training. The contribution therefore includes choices about how that analysis is carried out, alongside the overall training method.

The stated result is that these transformers can train large neural networks that are certifiably robust to adversarial perturbations. This links the precision of the underlying analysis with the scale of the learning procedure. The paper’s contribution is a scalable way to bring certification into network training, with multiple transformer designs for balancing the computational cost and precision of the robustness reasoning.
icml-2018-differentiable-abstract-interp.tldr: The paper uses abstract interpretation to train large neural networks with certified robustness while balancing computational efficiency and analysis precision.

paragraphs: Dynamic programming solves structured problems by combining solutions to smaller subproblems. Many such algorithms involve discrete choices that prevent ordinary differentiation, making them difficult to integrate into neural networks trained by backpropagation. This paper develops a way to turn a broad class of those algorithms into differentiable components.

The authors replace the maximum operation inside the recursion with a smoothed version defined using a strongly convex regularizer. This relaxes both the best objective value and the corresponding solution. Consequently, the structured computation can participate in gradient-based training. The analysis also gives a probabilistic interpretation of backpropagation through these operators and connects them with inference in graphical models.

Two concrete versions illustrate the framework: a smoothed Viterbi algorithm for sequence prediction and a smoothed dynamic time warping algorithm for time-series alignment. Applications include audio-to-score alignment, named entity recognition, and structured or sparse attention for translation. These examples demonstrate how structured algorithms can become trainable parts of neural models while retaining their problem-specific organization.
icml-2018-differentiable-dynamic-program.tldr: Smoothing dynamic programming recursions makes structured prediction and alignment algorithms differentiable components of neural networks.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a trained agent can continue learning efficiently from new experience. Its approach uses synaptic plasticity: connections can change as experience arrives. The authors show that the plasticity of Hebbian connections, alongside connection weights, can be optimized by gradient descent in recurrent networks containing millions of parameters.

This makes adaptation itself part of what training shapes. In an image-memory task, plastic recurrent networks with more than two million parameters learn to memorize and reconstruct sets of unfamiliar natural images containing over a thousand pixels. Traditional non-plastic recurrent networks fail to solve that task, providing evidence for the usefulness of plastic connections in the evaluated setting.

The authors also report competitive results on Omniglot meta-learning with little additional parameter cost. In reinforcement learning, plastic networks outperform corresponding non-plastic networks on maze exploration. Together, these findings support differentiable plasticity as a possible approach to learning how to learn: initial training prepares connection dynamics that can support later adaptation to new experience.
icml-2018-differentiable-plasticity-trai.tldr: Training connection plasticity with gradient descent enables recurrent networks to adapt through experience, with promising memory, meta-learning, and exploration results.

paragraphs: This paper develops generalization guarantees for training procedures that randomly perturb model parameters, with dropout as its main application. The central question is how randomness during training acts as regularization and how that effect depends on the data. The analysis expresses generalization error through two offset Rademacher complexity terms.

The main term incorporates a subtractive contribution from perturbation variance, capturing the regularizing effect. An auxiliary term controls how much that benefit can weaken. For neural networks, the authors introduce truthful dropout, a variant designed to preserve an unbiased output and fit the framework. They bound the variance it induces and connect those bounds with adaptive regularization.

For ReLU networks with one hidden layer, the framework yields a generalization upper bound without assumptions on parameter norms or the data distribution. The stated result combines a fast O(1/n) rate with adaptation to the geometry of the data points. Its significance is a mathematical account of how appropriately structured training randomness can produce data-sensitive generalization control.
icml-2018-dropout-training-data-dependen.tldr: A perturbation-based framework explains dropout’s data-dependent regularization and yields a fast generalization bound for one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.

paragraphs: This paper changes how a neural network’s weight matrices are represented. It uses low-dimensional vectors whose interactions through kernel functions determine the weights. The resulting architecture makes this interaction structure part of the model, providing a way to impose organization on the network through its parameterization.

The authors develop the theory behind the construction and show that a layer admits an interpretation involving an intermediate linear layer that can potentially be infinitely wide. This interpretation connects the compact vector representation with a much wider computational representation. The kernel functions mediate that connection, making the way vectors interact central to the architecture.

Concrete examples explore uses ranging from data visualization to recommender systems. The paper reports state-of-the-art performance on a MovieLens collaborative filtering task. That result supplies application-specific evidence for the architecture, while the broader contribution is the proposed way of structuring neural weights. It offers a common modeling idea that the authors investigate across several different types of application.
icml-2018-kernelized-synaptic-weight-mat.tldr: Kernel interactions between low-dimensional vectors parameterize neural weights, enabling structured architectures with strong reported collaborative filtering performance.

paragraphs: Training procedures can favor particular solutions even when a model has more parameters than it needs to fit the data. This paper studies that kind of implicit bias for dropout, a technique used to reduce overfitting. The aim is to understand the structure dropout encourages in the learned parameters.

The analysis focuses on linear neural networks with one hidden layer. In this setting, the authors show that dropout tends to equalize the norms of the incoming and outgoing weight vectors across hidden nodes. Norms measure the size of those vectors, so the result identifies a balancing tendency in how the network’s weights are distributed among its hidden units.

The paper also provides a complete characterization of the optimization landscape induced by dropout in the studied setting. This complements the balancing result by examining the objective that training must optimize. Together, the contributions give a mathematical description of dropout’s preference among parameter configurations, making its implicit bias more concrete for this particular network class.
icml-2018-on-the-implicit-bias-of-dropou.tldr: For single-hidden-layer linear networks, dropout favors balanced hidden-node weight norms and admits a complete optimization-landscape characterization.

paragraphs: Active learning can reduce labeling costs by choosing which examples receive labels, but its practical savings vary. This paper asks when uncertainty sampling is helpful for logistic regression. It defines data efficiency through the reduction in labeled examples needed to reach the same error rate, keeping predictive performance fixed when comparing labeling requirements.

Across 21 OpenML datasets, the authors find a strong inverse correlation between data efficiency and the final classifier’s error rate. In these experiments, greater labeling efficiency is associated with lower final error. This provides an empirical relationship between the achievable classification performance and the amount of benefit obtained from actively selecting data.

The theoretical result concerns a variant of uncertainty sampling and its asymptotic behavior. Its data efficiency lies within a constant factor of the inverse error rate of the limiting classifier. That qualified result gives mathematical support to the empirical pattern: in the analyzed regime, lower limiting error corresponds to greater efficiency on the inverse-error scale.
icml-2018-on-the-relationship-between-da.tldr: For logistic regression, experiments and an asymptotic analysis link uncertainty sampling’s labeling efficiency to the inverse of classifier error.

paragraphs: One-shot segmentation requires finding a previously unseen object and identifying its pixels from a single example. This paper studies the task in cluttered scenes and introduces cluttered Omniglot as a dataset. A baseline combines a Siamese embedding for detection with a U-net for segmentation, showing that more clutter makes the task harder.

The authors use oracle models with different amounts of ground-truth information to examine how the task’s parts interact. Their findings show that locating an object and separating it from its background are intertwined: better detection helps segmentation, and better segmentation helps detection. This motivates a model that gives the two processes opportunities to support each other.

The resulting MaskNet examines multiple candidate locations, proposes segmentations that mask away background clutter, and chooses among the segmented objects. The findings suggest that iteratively refining detection and foreground segmentation may help recognition in highly cluttered scenes. The contribution combines a dataset, an investigation of the task’s structure, and a model designed around that interaction.
icml-2018-one-shot-segmentation-in-clutt.tldr: MaskNet addresses one-shot segmentation in clutter by using candidate segmentations to help locate and select the requested object.

paragraphs: BLOSSOM addresses two decisions in optimization: how to choose the next function evaluation and when to stop searching. It combines Bayesian optimization with traditional local optimization. At each step, the algorithm selects among multiple acquisition functions and the local optimization option, making the choice of search strategy part of the procedure.

Acquisition functions guide which evaluation to request, while local optimization provides another way to pursue improvement. Allowing the algorithm to switch between them is intended to capture useful characteristics of both approaches. A stopping condition based on expected regret complements that selection mechanism, giving the search a principled criterion for deciding when further optimization is no longer required.

On a selection of optimization problems, the authors report efficient use of function evaluations and superior convergence toward the global minimum. Those findings concern the evaluated problems. The contribution brings search and stopping together: BLOSSOM adapts how it searches and halts when its expected-regret condition is fulfilled, treating both decisions as parts of one optimization process.
icml-2018-optimization-fast-and-slow-opt.tldr: BLOSSOM switches between Bayesian and local optimization strategies and uses expected regret to decide when to stop.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval is an important computational step in imaging systems, including applications that image beyond the diffraction limit or through scattering media. Noise makes the reconstruction problem difficult for traditional algorithms. Methods using signal priors can improve robustness, but the paper identifies a tradeoff: some restrict which measurement models they can support.

The proposed prDeep algorithm combines regularization by denoising with a convolutional neural network denoiser. This uses the denoising component to guide the reconstruction while seeking broad applicability across measurement systems. The approach targets both concerns together: resistance to noisy measurements and flexibility in the model describing how those measurements were produced.

The authors test prDeep in simulation and report robustness to noise across a variety of system models. This provides evidence that the proposed combination can address the tradeoff motivating the work. The stated validation is computational, and its significance is the demonstrated ability to use a neural denoiser within phase retrieval without restricting the algorithm to a single tested measurement model.
icml-2018-prdeep-robust-phase-retrieval-.tldr: prDeep combines a neural denoiser with regularization by denoising to achieve noise-robust phase retrieval across varied simulated system models.

paragraphs: Multitask learning can improve performance by sharing learned structure across related tasks. This paper asks whether some of that benefit can be obtained when only one task is available. Its answer is pseudo-task augmentation, a method that introduces multiple decoders for each task during training.

These decoders create pseudo-tasks intended to simulate training on closely related tasks from the same underlying universe. The method brings the idea of sharing within a task, making multiple decoders part of learning from the available task. The same construction can also be applied when several actual tasks are already being learned together.

Experiments show improvements on single-task learning problems. Combining pseudo-task augmentation with multitask learning yields further improvements, including reported state-of-the-art performance on CelebA. Those results support complementary value: the benefit of multiple decoders remains useful alongside sharing across actual tasks. The authors present the method as an efficient, broadly applicable way to improve deep learning systems through the organization of their training.
icml-2018-pseudo-task-augmentation-from-.tldr: Training multiple decoders per task improves single-task learning and provides complementary gains when combined with multitask learning.

paragraphs: The paper introduces probability models for rankings by imagining that rankings are generated through a noisy sorting procedure. Each comparison between two items becomes a Bernoulli trial instead of a deterministic decision. The comparison probabilities can be interpreted as pairwise preferences, connecting local choices between items to probabilities over complete rankings.

When the sorting procedure is insertion sort or quicksort, the authors show that the resulting model has a closed-form expression. They propose maximum likelihood estimation to learn its parameters from observed ranking data. This gives the sorting-based construction both a probabilistic interpretation and a concrete route for fitting the model.

A generalized version relaxes constraints on the pairwise preferences and uses a variation of generalized iterative scaling for maximum likelihood estimation. Experiments report strong goodness of fit compared with existing ranking models. The findings support noisy sorting as a useful statistical construction: a familiar algorithmic process becomes a mechanism for describing variation across observed orderings.
icml-2018-ranking-distributions-based-on.tldr: Noisy sorting procedures define learnable probability distributions over rankings, with strong reported fit compared with existing models.

paragraphs: The paper studies rapid adaptation: changing a neural network’s behavior for a new task using little task experience. It introduces conditionally shifted neurons within a meta-learning framework, where training aims to prepare a model for adaptation. The mechanism makes task-specific changes directly to the activation values of neurons.

Those changes are shifts retrieved from a memory module. Limited experience with the current task quickly populates that memory, which then supplies the information used to modify activations. This gives the model a concrete pathway from a small amount of new experience to a change in its computation: task information is stored and subsequently expressed through neuron activations.

Models augmented with conditionally shifted neurons achieve reported state-of-the-art results on meta-learning benchmarks in vision and language. The evidence therefore spans two application domains for the proposed adaptation mechanism. The contribution is a way of incorporating quickly acquired task information into neural computation, with benchmark results supporting its usefulness for learning new tasks from limited data.
icml-2018-rapid-adaptation-with-conditio.tldr: Conditionally shifted neurons use memory-derived activation shifts to adapt quickly to new tasks, with strong vision and language meta-learning results.

paragraphs: The paper revisits stochastic principal component analysis through convex relaxation. Although direct nonconvex methods have strong efficiency results, convex approaches have shown competitive or better empirical behavior. This motivates a closer theoretical study of how to improve stochastic optimization within the convex formulation.

The authors investigate stochastic gradient methods with three forms of regularization. The ℓ2 variant targets better iteration complexity, the ℓ1 variant targets control over the rank of intermediate iterates, and elastic net combines the two motivations. These choices address both progress toward the objective and the structure of the objects maintained during optimization.

Theory and experiments show faster convergence and lower runtime to reach a user-specified objective accuracy compared with earlier convex-relaxation methods. The methods converge in both PCA objective value and distance between subspaces, linking numerical optimization progress with recovery of the desired subspace. A computational gap relative to existing nonconvex approaches remains, so the improvement strengthens the convex approach without eliminating that stated difference.
icml-2018-stochastic-pca-with-ell-2-and-.tldr: Regularized stochastic methods accelerate convex-relaxation PCA, although their computational requirements still lag existing nonconvex approaches.

paragraphs: Distributed training can include adversarial workers that send poisoned gradients. Some aggregation schemes guarantee convergence despite a minority of such workers. This paper shows why that guarantee alone is insufficient: in high-dimensional, nonconvex learning problems, an attacker can still steer convergence toward an ineffective model.

The authors identify poisoning freedom in existing schemes that grows with dimension, with a lower bound increasing at least as a pth root of the dimension. They use that freedom to construct a simple attack and demonstrate strong effects on CIFAR-10 and MNIST. The vulnerability concerns where training ends up, even when the optimization process technically converges.

The proposed Bulyan method provably reduces the attacker’s leeway to an O(1/√d) bound. Experiments show that it avoids the observed fragility of existing aggregation rules and achieves convergence resembling training with only non-adversarial gradients, at a reported reasonable batch-size cost. The work connects a dimension-dependent theoretical vulnerability with an attack and a method designed to sharply restrict it.
icml-2018-the-hidden-vulnerability-of-di.tldr: The paper shows that Byzantine-resilient convergence can still yield ineffective models and introduces Bulyan to sharply reduce poisoning freedom.

paragraphs: A new observation in a data stream might fit the existing distribution, be an isolated outlier, or mark the start of a different distribution. This paper addresses that ambiguity with a hierarchical Bayesian algorithm. It aims to maintain a time-specific approximate posterior over the parameters describing the observed data.

For models in the exponential family, the authors derive equations that update the variational parameters at each time step. They connect these updates to reinforcement learning. In that interpretation, the model learns its posterior according to a confidence in stability, while that confidence is itself learned according to another level of stability confidence.

This hierarchy makes the treatment of stability part of the learning process. It provides a framework for adapting beliefs as observations arrive while also updating confidence in how stable the underlying process is. The authors demonstrate applications in reinforcement learning, an adaptive Bayesian autoregressive model, and stochastic gradient descent optimization, illustrating the reach of the same generic formulation across these settings.
icml-2018-the-hierarchical-adaptive-forg.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian filter updates beliefs about streaming data while learning nested levels of confidence in the process’s stability.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether additional supervision on interpretable internal parts of neural machines improves training. Such supervision supplies guidance through traces of computation. The question is whether that extra information helps existing neural machine architectures converge and generalize more effectively than their standard training procedures.

To formalize which architectures can use this approach, the authors introduce differential neural computational machines. They show that existing Neural Turing Machines and Neural Random Access Machines fit within this class. The definition provides a common framework for discussing trace-based supervision across those architectures and identifying the parts of their computation to which supervision can apply.

A detailed experimental evaluation on both machine types finds better convergence and generalization with the additional supervision. The improvements appear in both noise-free and noisy scenarios. These findings support using interpretable internal computation as a training resource when such supervision is available. The contribution combines a framework describing eligible machines with empirical evidence that supervising their internal behavior can improve learning.
icml-2018-training-neural-machines-with-.tldr: Supervising interpretable internal computations improves convergence and generalization in evaluated Neural Turing Machines and Neural Random Access Machines.

paragraphs: The paper examines when GAN training converges, particularly when data and generator distributions occupy lower-dimensional structures. A simple counterexample shows that unregularized training need not converge without absolute continuity. This demonstrates why a distributional requirement in earlier convergence results cannot simply be removed.

The analysis finds convergence for training with instance noise or zero-centered gradient penalties. It also shows that Wasserstein GANs and WGAN-GP do not always reach equilibrium when only finitely many discriminator updates are performed per generator update. These results distinguish the behavior of particular stabilization methods and update settings, helping explain why apparently reasonable GAN training procedures can remain unstable.

The authors extend their analysis to more general GANs and prove local convergence with simplified gradient penalties even when the generator and data distributions lie on lower-dimensional manifolds. Local convergence concerns behavior near an equilibrium. In practice, the penalties work well for high-resolution image generation across several datasets with little hyperparameter tuning, connecting the theoretical analysis with useful training behavior.
icml-2018-which-training-methods-for-gan.tldr: Counterexamples expose GAN convergence failures, while simplified gradient penalties provide local convergence guarantees even for distributions on lower-dimensional manifolds.

paragraphs: Sparse linear models with pairwise interactions can capture relationships that individual features alone do not express. However, the number of possible pairs grows quadratically with the number of features. This makes conventional ℓ1-regularized implementations difficult to scale to genetic datasets containing hundreds of thousands of features.

WHInter addresses this problem with a working-set algorithm for binary design matrices. It focuses optimization on selected variables, using a new bound to identify working sets efficiently without scanning all features. It also incorporates fast computations inspired by maximum inner product search. These components target the cost of finding relevant interactions within the enormous candidate space.

Tests on simulated and real genetic data show greater scalability and a reported speed improvement of two orders of magnitude over the state of the art. The method’s scope includes the stated binary-matrix setting. Its contribution is a computational strategy that makes large sparse interaction models more tractable by reducing the search work required to assemble and update useful working sets.
icml-2018-whinter-a-working-set-algorith.tldr: WHInter efficiently selects working sets for sparse pairwise-interaction models on binary data, reporting substantially better scalability and roughly hundredfold speedups.
